title: Feedback That Changes What People Do
performance: The viewer takes one piece of feedback they were about to give and rewrites it into three parts: a specific observed behaviour, its effect, and a next step the other person can try, then picks a calm, soon-after moment to deliver it as a two-way conversation.

audience.assumed_prior: Knows feedback matters and gives it regularly, but tends to say something vague like 'be more proactive' and hopes it lands.
audience.why: Corporate employees who give feedback to peers or reports; prior knowledge of the habit is high, of a usable structure is low.
audience.motivation: Wants a real change in how a colleague works without damaging the relationship.
audience.context: Short self-paced corporate video, watched between tasks; the viewer has a real feedback moment coming up.

strategy.name: worked_example_led
strategy.rationale: Practitioners need a usable structure fast. One running scene (a team meeting and one colleague) is reworked in front of them, then they run the same move on a fresh remark and on their own. Expertise reversal: one short worked example, then a decision, then their own case.
strategy.signature_move: Show the vague remark, strip the label, add the observed behaviour, add its effect, add the agreed next step, then the viewer repeats it.

misconceptions.belief: A warm, vague remark like 'be a bit more engaged' is the kind way to give feedback, and it tells the person what to do.
misconceptions.why_tempting: It feels good to say and to hear, and the label seems self-explanatory to the giver.

misconceptions.belief: Being specific is harsh: kind and effective feedback pull in opposite directions.
misconceptions.why_tempting: Naming a behaviour feels like confrontation, so softening into labels feels safer for the relationship.

hook.sketch: Imagine a manager tells a colleague, 'Great job, just be a bit more engaged.' He glows, and by the next meeting nothing has changed. On screen: the remark as a fuzzy cloud over two people in a meeting room.

arc.promise: Same remark, same meeting: by the end you will have turned it into feedback your colleague can actually act on, and you will have rewritten one of your own.
arc.bridge_from_prior: Think of the last feedback you gave. You probably liked how it felt to say. Did anyone do anything different afterwards?

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why vague or purely pleasant feedback feels good yet tends to give the person nothing to act on
concepts: F2 comfortable to give and receive, little to act on
F4 a label describes an impression
F3 feedback aimed at the person tends to be less useful than about a task or action
sections.carrier: story scene: the opening meeting room, the remark as a fuzzy cloud over the colleague; the glow fades
sections.recap_after: the cloud tells him how he came across, not what to do on Tuesday

sections.goal: the viewer can apply three parts, observed behaviour, effect and a next step agreed together, to rework the opening remark
concepts: F5 observable behaviour is what a camera would capture
F6 behaviour without guessing motive is easier to recognise
F7 effect on the work or team, stated honestly
F8 next step is a small action for the next opportunity
F9 agreed together tends to work better than imposed
F13 one common model, others exist
sections.carrier: one board built up by additions: the cloud sharpens into three labelled parts, each named after it appears; what CHANGES is the fuzzy label being replaced by a behaviour line, then an effect line, then a next-step line
sections.recap_after: behaviour, effect, next step: a camera could see the first, the team feels the second, the third is for the next meeting

sections.goal: the viewer can distinguish which of two versions of a new remark a colleague could act on, and say why
concepts: Specific behaviour, effect and next step versus a warm label
F2, F4, F5 applied to a fresh remark
sections.carrier: split-screen choice card with two remarks, then an answer card; the quiz pauses before the answer
sections.recap_after: the one you can picture on camera is the one a colleague can change

sections.goal: the viewer can schedule a calm, private moment soon after the event and use an opening question to turn the feedback into a two-way conversation
concepts: F10 soon after, calm and private rather than in the heat of the moment or in public
F11 ask for their view and listen, they may know context you do not
F12 kind and effective are compatible
sections.carrier: calm one-to-one scene: the two colleagues sitting side by side with a coffee, a speech bubble with a question; what changes is the colleague's turn to speak
sections.recap_after: soon, private, and ask before you conclude

sections.goal: the viewer can apply the three parts to one real piece of upcoming feedback and choose when to deliver it, then see the opening meeting handled
concepts: Transfer: rewrite own remark in three parts
Payoff: before and after of the opening meeting
sections.carrier: direct-to-camera prompt with an empty three-part board, then the before-and-after of the opening meeting
sections.recap_after: your remark, three parts, a moment this week

arc.payoff: Back in the opening meeting: same colleague, now given the reworked feedback in three parts. In the next meeting he does the specific thing agreed, and the two of them are still on good terms. The glow was never the point; the change was.

practice_ladder.task: Watch the opening remark rebuilt into behaviour, effect and next step, each part named after it appears.
Choose which of two new remarks a colleague could act on, after pausing, then see why.
Rewrite one real upcoming piece of feedback in the three parts and pick when to deliver it.

recall_moments.question: Which remark could a colleague act on?
options: A: 'You need to be a stronger team player in meetings.'
B: 'In today's meeting you gave one-word answers on the vendor question, so we lost your view before deciding. Next time, could you share a view before we decide?'
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: A, because it sounds warm and the wording feels kinder, though it is a label the colleague cannot picture or act on.

recall_moments.prompt: Remember the camera test from the board? Run your own remark past it: could a recording show it?

transfer_tasks.task: Take one piece of feedback you were about to give. Rewrite it as one observed behaviour, its effect, and a small next step you would agree together. Pick a calm, private moment soon after and write the opening question you will ask.
transfer_tasks.context: Their own real feedback to a peer or report this week.

gagne.recall_prior: arc.bridge_from_prior, the viewer's last feedback moment
gagne.guidance: strategy.signature_move and the worked rebuild in s2_three_parts
gagne.practice: pacing.recall_moments (quiz after s2_three_parts, recall_prompt after s3_check) and practice_ladder

merrill.problem_centred: one running scene, the vague remark in the team meeting, runs from hook to payoff
merrill.activation: bridge_from_prior asks about the viewer's own recent feedback
merrill.demonstration: s2_three_parts rebuilds the remark in front of the viewer
merrill.application: quiz in s3_check and own rewrite in s5_your_turn
merrill.integration: transfer_tasks and delivery timing in s4_timing_talk and s5_your_turn

mayer.coherence: one loud thing on screen at a time, no decorative extras
mayer.signalling: each part is named after it appears, highlighted on the board
mayer.redundancy: on-screen text is the short remark lines only, narration carries the explanation
mayer.contiguity: each part's label appears beside the line it names
mayer.segmenting: five short sections, each one idea
mayer.pretraining: s1_gap shows why the label fails before the parts are introduced

arcs.attention: familiar warm remark that fades with no change
arcs.relevance: the viewer's own upcoming feedback conversation
arcs.confidence: three small parts, one worked example, a binary check before their own attempt
arcs.satisfaction: payoff shows the colleague changing and the relationship intact

flags: RECALL-NOTE: the quiz is placed after s2_three_parts and presented in s3_check, which holds only the question and answer cards.
ENERGY-NOTE: no rest section can exceed 180 s in a 120 s video; s4_timing_talk is the single rest valley (about 15 s).

OPEN-QUESTION: the knowledge sheet anchors the three parts as one common model (F13, behaviour-impact models such as SBI) and the audience mix of peers or reports is not settled, so wording stays neutral between the two.
UNVERIFIED: knowledge sheet was not verified against the Kluger and DeNisi (1996) or CCL SBI originals; narration should say 'tends to' and avoid figures.
